poems.title: The Lamp Song
poems.author: Ilsabet Corrow
lines: Light one lamp and name one thing,
Then light another, name it too.
The Tide goes by on a silver wing
And finds the whole street holding true.

poems.title: The Small Door
poems.author: Fennimore Dray
lines: A small green door beside the stair
Keeps all the things I left in there.
I knock, I say each one aloud,
And out they come, a patient crowd.

poems.title: Morning Count
poems.author: Tavish Lorn
lines: One for the kettle, two for the bread,
Three for the lamp above my head,
Four for the window, five for the sun:
I counted my morning, and it was done.

poems.title: Boats at the Quay
poems.author: Odile Harrowmere
lines: The Tide comes in at close of day
And sweeps the little things away.
But what I name, and what I see,
Stays tied like boats along the quay.
I tie one more, and then one more,
Until a fleet fills up the shore.

poems.title: Wren's Rule
poems.author: Marit Ashvane
lines: Write it small and say it plain,
Then walk it through your house again.
Close the book and tell it through,
Each stop in turn, from old to new.
If one has slipped, then look, and then
Close the book and try again.

poems.title: The Archive Cat
poems.author: Brannoc Pell
lines: The Archive cat has read no book,
Yet knows each shelf and every nook.
She sleeps upon the oldest page
And does not mind the weight of age.
At dusk she walks the stacks, and I
Go with her, tail and lamp held high.

poems.title: The House Count
poems.author: Sorrel Wick
lines: One for the lamp that burns by the door,
Two for the boots that wait on the floor.
Three for the cups on the kitchen shelf,
Four for the cat who has found herself.
Five for the window that frames the hill,
Six for the clock that is never still.
Seven for the stairs that creak at night,
Eight for the candle that lends its light.

poems.title: Twelve Gates
poems.author: Sorrel Wick
lines: Twelve gates stand along the river,
Each one hung with its own lamp.
Some are bright and some a-shiver,
Some are quiet, some are damp.
Walk them slowly, one by one,
Say what each one holds for you.
When the evening mist has come,
You will know the whole road through.

poems.title: Counting Stairs
poems.author: Isaure Fenn
lines: Down below the Archive floor
The stairs go on and on and on.
Every step has one thing more
To remember, and then it's gone,
Unless I set it in a place
And give it legs, a hat, a name.
Then when the mist comes round my face
It stands up straight and says, "I came."

poems.title: Salt and Lamp Oil
poems.author: Brannoc Pell
lines: Salt for the bread and oil for the lamp,
A coil of rope and a roll of twine,
Two bright coins and a postage stamp,
A pen, a shell, a sprig of pine.
I lay them down along the wall,
One at each stone, and I walk away.
Tomorrow I will find them all
Exactly where they lay today.

poems.title: The Long Walk Home
poems.author: Ilsabet Corrow
lines: When the evening lamps come on
I walk the road I know by heart:
The baker's door, the elm, the swan
Of stone, the fountain, and the cart.
Then comes the gate, the crooked house,
The leaning wall, the well, the stair.
I never hurry, and I rouse
Each one by name and leave it there.
At last I reach my own front door,
The key, the latch, the kitchen light.
And every place I passed before
Is waiting for me through the night.

poems.title: The Forgiving River
poems.author: Tavish Lorn
lines: The river takes what I forget,
And that is all right, and that is fair.
It does not scold me, does not fret,
It only wonders, "Was it there?"
So I go back and look again
And ask the lamp to light the place.
The river hums an old refrain:
"There is no hurry in this race."
I hold it gently, not too tight,
And hand it over to the dawn.
Tomorrow it will still be light,
And I will find it. On and on.

poems.title: Three Wishes for a Keeper
poems.author: Marit Ashvane
lines: May your pictures be absurd,
May they wobble, jump and sing,
May you hold each silly word
Like a coin upon a string.
May your places stay in line,
Door and window, shelf and chair,
May the thing you left be fine
When you come to find it there.
May you rest, and may you play,
May the lamp be always lit,
May you finish every day
Glad of what you did with it.

poems.title: The Lamplighter's Round
poems.author: Odile Harrowmere
lines: The market closes, one by one
The shutters come down in the square.
The last of the light on the stones is gone,
And the lamplighter climbs her stair.
She lights the first above the well,
The second at the old bell tower,
The third where the river willows tell
Their secrets at this hour.
And I, who walk the evening round,
Say every name as I go past,
The well, the bell, the willow ground,
And keep them safe and fast.
Then home, and in my little room
I count them over, light by light,
And watch the last one's silver bloom
Dissolve into the night.

poems.title: What I Know About Mist
poems.author: Brannoc Pell
lines: Mist knows no door and no wall,
It comes in under all the sills.
It is not angry, not at all,
It only does what the river wills.
It takes the shape of what is near
And makes each hedge a sleeping beast.
It hides the road, it hides the pier,
It hides the greatest and the least.
But mist is only water, thin,
And thin things lift when morning comes.
The sun pulls gently, and the din
Of birds goes up like distant drums.
So when the mist is in your head
And every name goes soft and blurred,
Just set a lamp where you have led
Each picture, and say each word.

poems.title: Rain
poems.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
lines: The rain is raining all around,
It falls on field and tree,
It rains on the umbrellas here,
And on the ships at sea.

poems.title: A word is dead
poems.author: Emily Dickinson
lines: A word is dead
When it is said,
Some say.
I say it just
Begins to live
That day.

poems.title: Who Has Seen the Wind?
poems.author: Christina Rossetti
lines: Who has seen the wind?
Neither I nor you:
But when the leaves hang trembling
The wind is passing thro'.
Who has seen the wind?
Neither you nor I:
But when the trees bow down their heads
The wind is passing by.

poems.title: Jenny Kiss'd Me
poems.author: Leigh Hunt
lines: Jenny kiss'd me when we met,
Jumping from the chair she sat in;
Time, you thief, who love to get
Sweets into your list, put that in!
Say I'm weary, say I'm sad,
Say that health and wealth have miss'd me,
Say I'm growing old, but add,
Jenny kiss'd me.

line 4: Sweets into your list, put that in:

poems.title: There is no Frigate like a Book
poems.author: Emily Dickinson
lines: There is no frigate like a book
To take us lands away,
Nor any coursers like a page
Of prancing poetry.
This traverse may the poorest take
Without oppress of toll;
How frugal is the chariot
That bears a human soul!

poems.title: The Swing
poems.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
lines: How do you like to go up in a swing,
Up in the air so blue?
Oh, I do think it the pleasantest thing
Ever a child can do!
Up in the air and over the wall,
Till I can see so wide,
Rivers and trees and cattle and all
Over the countryside—
Till I look down on the garden green,
Down on the roof so brown—
Up in the air I go flying again,
Up in the air and down!

poems.title: Bed in Summer
poems.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
lines: In winter I get up at night
And dress by yellow candle-light.
In summer, quite the other way,
I have to go to bed by day.
I have to go to bed and see
The birds still hopping on the tree,
Or hear the grown-up people's feet
Still going past me in the street.
And does it not seem hard to you,
When all the sky is clear and blue,
And I should like so much to play,
To have to go to bed by day?

poems.title: The Arrow and the Song
poems.author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
lines: I shot an arrow into the air,
It fell to earth, I knew not where;
For, so swiftly it flew, the sight
Could not follow it in its flight.
I breathed a song into the air,
It fell to earth, I knew not where;
For who has sight so keen and strong,
That it can follow the flight of song?
Long, long afterward, in an oak
I found the arrow, still unbroke;
And the song, from beginning to end,
I found again in the heart of a friend.

poems.title: To the Virgins, to Make Much of Time
poems.author: Robert Herrick
lines: Gather ye rosebuds while ye may,
Old Time is still a-flying:
And this same flower that smiles to-day
To-morrow will be dying.
The glorious lamp of heaven, the sun,
The higher he's a-getting,
The sooner will his race be run,
And nearer he's to setting.
That age is best which is the first,
When youth and blood are warmer;
But being spent, the worse, and worst
Times still succeed the former.
Then be not coy, but use your time,
And while ye may, go marry:
For having lost but once your prime,
You may for ever tarry.

line 14: And while ye may go marry:
line 15: For having lost but once your prime

poems.title: To Celia
poems.author: Ben Jonson
lines: Drink to me only with thine eyes,
And I will pledge with mine;
Or leave a kiss but in the cup
And I'll not look for wine.
The thirst that from the soul doth rise
Doth ask a drink divine;
But might I of Jove's nectar sup,
I would not change for thine.
I sent thee late a rosy wreath,
Not so much honouring thee
As giving it a hope that there
It could not wither'd be;
But thou thereon didst only breathe,
And sent'st it back to me;
Since when it grows, and smells, I swear,
Not of itself but thee!

line 3: Or leave a kiss but in the cup,

poems.title: A Birthday
poems.author: Christina Rossetti
lines: My heart is like a singing bird
Whose nest is in a watered shoot;
My heart is like an apple-tree
Whose boughs are bent with thickset fruit;
My heart is like a rainbow shell
That paddles in a halcyon sea;
My heart is gladder than all these
Because my love is come to me.
Raise me a dais of silk and down;
Hang it with vair and purple dyes;
Carve it in doves and pomegranates,
And peacocks with a hundred eyes;
Work it in gold and silver grapes,
In leaves and silver fleurs-de-lys;
Because the birthday of my life
Is come, my love is come to me.

line 3: My heart is like an appletree
line 4: Whose boughs are bent with thick-set fruit;
line 11: Carve it in doves, and pomegranates,

poems.title: Crossing the Bar
poems.author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
lines: Sunset and evening star,
And one clear call for me!
And may there be no moaning of the bar,
When I put out to sea,
But such a tide as moving seems asleep,
Too full for sound and foam,
When that which drew from out the boundless deep
Turns again home.
Twilight and evening bell,
And after that the dark!
And may there be no sadness of farewell,
When I embark;
For tho' from out our bourne of Time and Place
The flood may bear me far,
I hope to see my Pilot face to face
When I have crost the bar.

line 16: When I have cross'd the bar.

poems.title: Remember
poems.author: Christina Rossetti
lines: Remember me when I am gone away,
Gone far away into the silent land;
When you can no more hold me by the hand,
Nor I half turn to go yet turning stay.
Remember me when no more day by day
You tell me of our future that you planned:
Only remember me; you understand
It will be late to counsel then or pray.
Yet if you should forget me for a while
And afterwards remember, do not grieve:
For if the darkness and corruption leave
A vestige of the thoughts that once I had,
Better by far you should forget and smile
Than that you should remember and be sad.

poems.title: Sonnet 18
poems.author: William Shakespeare
lines: Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?
Thou art more lovely and more temperate:
Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May,
And summer's lease hath all too short a date:
Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines,
And often is his gold complexion dimm'd,
And every fair from fair sometime declines,
By chance, or nature's changing course untrimm'd:
But thy eternal summer shall not fade,
Nor lose possession of that fair thou ow'st,
Nor shall death brag thou wander'st in his shade,
When in eternal lines to time thou grow'st,
So long as men can breathe, or eyes can see,
So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.

learn.1: Make a tiny palace of four stops, such as the door, the hall mirror, the sofa and the kitchen sink. Line 1: a green door, with a stair beside it, stands at your first stop. Line 2: at the mirror, a crowd of your lost things are packed inside. Line 3: at the sofa, you knock and shout each one aloud. Line 4: at the sink, a patient crowd climbs out. Walk the four stops, say each line, close the page, and walk them again. Practise this once and the whole poem usually holds for the day.
learn.2: Take the three pairs of lines as three pictures and chain them. Pair 1: the Tide sweeps little things off a table. Pair 2: you tie each thing you name to a small boat at a quay. Pair 3: a whole fleet fills the shore. Link the pictures with one action each, then say the poem aloud while you move through them. Use the first word of every line as your cue when you check yourself: The, And, But, Stays, I, Until.
learn.3: Use a palace of four stops and two lines at each. Stop 1: a salt shaker pours bread and lamp oil (lines 1 and 2: salt, oil, rope, twine). Stop 2: two coins and a stamp are stuck to a pen, a shell and a pine sprig (lines 3 and 4). Stop 3: you lay everything out along a wall, one object at each stone (lines 5 and 6). Stop 4: tomorrow you find them all in the same place (lines 7 and 8). Pictures hold the ideas. The rhymes (lamp and stamp, twine and pine, wall and all, away and today) hold the exact words, so say the rhyming pairs aloud as you walk.
learn.4: Treat each stanza as one room with four things in it. Stanza 1 is the front hall (baker, elm, stone swan, fountain, cart); stanza 2 is the garden (gate, crooked house, wall, well, stair); stanza 3 is the kitchen (key, latch, light). First learn only the first word of every line (When, I, The, Of, Then, The, I, Each, At, The, And, Is). Then add the rest, one room a night. Check before you look: say a stanza from memory, then compare, and only then re-read.
learn.5: Give each of the four stanzas its own room and put one strong picture on every line, so sixteen pictures in four rooms. Learn one stanza a night, then on the fifth night link the four rooms in order and recite the whole poem without stopping. Say it again after a day, after a week and after a month (the game schedules these checks). For a strict page, practise the capitals and the marks too: write the poem out line by line and compare, because only exact copies count.
